newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Political jitters hold back HK economic recovery.
newsitem.headline: Political jitters hold back HK economic recovery.

text.p: Hong Kong's economy is gaining ground, but uncertainty associated with the return of the British colony to Chinese rule next year continues to weigh on any improvements, economists said on Wednesday.

"I think we are becoming increasingly confident that a recovery is in the making and in some sectors it has already begun...but so far what we have seen is very mild," said Charles Li, chief economist at Natwest Markets.

Stronger retail sales, flat inflation and a more spirited property market all suggest the Hong Kong economy is bottoming out after a three-year decline, but few expect to see a solid recovery until after the handover.
Confidence is considered the key to further strength.

Economists said everybody in Hong Kong, from ordinary people to large corporations, needed solid proof that the 1997 transition would proceed smoothly before opening their wallets and coffers to allow Hong Kong's economy to race ahead.

"There is a feeling that once this uncertainty is removed the rebound potential here in confidence could be very fast, but until you have those actions there are always going to be those lingering doubts," said Bob Broadfoot, managing director at the Political and Economic Risk Consultancy.
Some economists said a recent uptick in retail sales and more activity in Hong Kong's volatile property market suggested the economy had at least stopped weakening.

"There's been a slight recovery in the second quarter which will probably continue into the third and fourth quarters and through 1997, but it's only a slight recovery," said Ian Perkin, chief economist at the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.
But other economists said the recent strength in retail sales boded well for 1997.
Retail sales gained by 0.7 percent in the second quarter compared to 0.1 percent in the first quarter. They also rose 2.6 percent in July, the first month of the third quarter.

"There is an upwards trend, both in private consumption and retail sales," said George Leung, economist at Hongkong Bank. "It all points to recovery in the domestic sector and seems to be pointing to a positive rather than negative prospect."
Countering these promising signs are sluggish economic growth, which is expected to remain below five percent this year, and a bleak outlook for exports.

"I don't know that we can expect much," said Perkin. "If the U.S. is slowing down, there won't be much demand there, and if you look at exports by country in Hong Kong this year, the only really big growth area has been Japan."

One of the most promising indicators is the Hong Kong stock market, which has reached new peaks lately and prompted speculation that investors are removing some political discount in anticipation of an easy transition.

"Here we see the disparity between the real economy and financial markets," said Li at Natwest. "The real economy depends a lot more on investment and consumption by locals while in the financial markets, the foreign funds have been playing a significant role."
Other Hong Kong commentators said local investors seem to be playing a waiting game, taking only slight comfort from the recent defrost in Sino-British relations.
"I think people are very leery about next year," said Christopher Hammerbeck, executive director with the British Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong.
"On the whole, people are being quite leery about committing themselves to any financing or major expenditure 12 months ahead."
